top_choice_rationale: P003 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) credits a mature, roughly thirty-year programme that made electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity objects of formal and empirical analysis, with a clear link to fiscal policy and public-goods provision. A citation worded around rules and fiscal outcomes distinguishes it from the 2024 prize on the historical origins of institutions. Its weaknesses are weaker identification in the early cross-country work and a Persson-Tabellini / Besley-Persson credit boundary that cannot be cleanly separated, so the margin over P002 is narrow. P002 has the cleanest two-person attribution but mixed confirmation of protection-for-sale. P001 has the widest empirical footprint but an unresolved credit boundary with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum. P004 has the strongest design-based evidence, but the magnitude and persistence of the effects are debated and the task-framework attribution is messy. Any of the four awards is preferable to no award.
recusal_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Persson, Tabellini or Besley is apparent from the profile. My own research on dynamic political economy (welfare state, dynamics of government) is thematically adjacent to P003. I recall, without verification, that Persson has long been associated with IIES; this is not in the profile. I have co-authored with committee colleagues Krusell, Boppart and Friberg, who are not candidates, and agreement with them is not independent evidence. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
